# Ticket Triage

`customer_support.intake_and_triage.ticket_triage` · v1.0.0 · **draft**

**What is this, how bad is it, and whose queue can actually finish it?**


> Reading a newly arrived contact and deciding, fast and on partial evidence, what kind of work it is, how badly it is hurting and whom, and which queue can actually finish it. Triage is a routing decision, not an analysis: its job is to place the ticket where the next useful act can happen, not to be right about the cause. Its defining property is that the cost of a wrong route is paid three steps later by someone who cannot undo it — the clock has already run, the customer has already been told who owns it, and the framing set at triage tends to survive every subsequent hand. The discipline is therefore holding severity apart from priority, checking what the account is entitled to before believing what the ticket says about itself, and making an unestablished severity fail toward attention rather than away from it.

## Expertise applied


## Outcomes

- The contact is classified as a kind of work — question, defect, request, or account matter — rather than by the subject line it arrived under.
- Severity is recorded as a property of the fault: established from what is broken, for how many, and whether a customer-executable workaround exists.
- Priority is recorded as a separate decision about scarce attention, with the entitlement and account context that produced it visible to whoever inherits the ticket.
- An owning queue is named, and it is the queue that can close the ticket rather than the queue that will understand it first.
- Where severity could not be established, the ticket carries an explicit unknown that routes toward attention — never a silent default that routes it downward.
- The triage note states what was assumed and what would change the verdict, so the next agent can disagree with the assumption instead of re-deriving it.
- Where the same fault has already been reported, the relationship is recorded before the second ticket is worked, because volume is severity evidence.


## Failure modes

- Triaging on the loudest sentence in the ticket. Tone measures the state of the relationship and almost nothing about the state of the fault, yet it is the most reliable predictor of how a queue actually sorts — which teaches customers that escalation language works and destroys the signal for everyone who did not use it.
- Collapsing severity into priority. Once they are one field, the enterprise account with a cosmetic defect and the trial user with data loss get the same verdict and both are wrong, and the organisation loses the ability to even express the inversion.
- Letting unknown severity fall to the bottom. Unknown is not low; it is unmeasured. The contacts that become incidents are disproportionately the ones nobody could classify in the first minute, because unusual shape is exactly what a taxonomy fails on.
- Routing to the team that owns the surface rather than the team that owns the cause. Customers report where they noticed the failure, and the page where it surfaced is frequently owned by a team with no access to the system that broke.
- Triaging without opening the entitlement. What the account is owed is invisible in the ticket text, and it is the first thing a fast triager skips, because skipping it costs nothing today.
- Re-triage churn. Every hop resets the perceived clock in the receiving agent's head while the real clock keeps running, so a ticket bounced twice is often already late at the moment someone finally owns it.
- Silent downgrade. Moving a ticket to a slower queue without recording that a priority decision was made converts a judgement into an accident, and nothing about it can be reviewed afterwards.
- Treating a duplicate as a fresh contact. Independent triage of the same fault destroys the only early evidence that blast radius is growing, and blast radius is the input that turns a ticket into an incident.
- Batch triage at the start of a shift. It optimises the triager's context-switching and maximises the age of everything in the batch — the wrong variable to optimise when the clock starts at submission.
- Triaging to a specialist queue for comprehension. It produces a chain of well-informed people who each lack the permission, the access or the code to finish the work.
- Perfect triage. Time spent resolving genuine ambiguity past the point of diminishing return is time the clock is spending, and a provisional route with a stated assumption beats a correct route arrived at late.


## KPIs

| KPI | Unit | Direction | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| first_route_accuracy | percent | higher_is_better | Share of tickets closed by the queue they were first routed to. Reads as a measure of the triager and is mostly a measure of the taxonomy. |
| reassignments_per_ticket | count | lower_is_better | How many owners a ticket collects before someone finishes it. The clearest single symptom of a routing model that does not fit the work. |
| time_to_triage | minutes | lower_is_better | Submission to first routing decision. Measured from submission, never from the moment an agent opened the ticket — the second version hides the entire queueing problem. |
| severity_revision_rate | percent | target_band | Share of tickets whose severity changed after triage. Near zero means severity is being copied forward rather than established; very high means it is being guessed. |
| unknown_severity_share | percent | target_band | Share triaged with severity explicitly unestablished. Meaningless alone — read only alongside what subsequently happened to those tickets. |
| escalation_shortly_after_triage | percent | lower_is_better | Tickets escalated soon after being triaged. Mostly a census of triage misses, occasionally a genuine signal that the system is degrading faster than intake can see. |
| duplicate_link_rate | percent | higher_is_better | Share of tickets correctly related to an existing issue at triage time. Low values mean blast radius is being discovered by engineering instead of by the queue. |
| triage_reversal_by_review | percent | lower_is_better | Share of triage verdicts a later quality review disagrees with. Measures whether the written standard and the practised standard are the same standard. |

> Note what is deliberately absent: no severity bands, no ageing thresholds, no reassignment limits, no weighting between entitlement and blast radius. All of that is Layer 4 arithmetic and belongs in the pack manifest; a number appearing here would mean the Layer 3/4 boundary had leaked. Note also what this capability cannot currently see — there is no ticket, SLA or escalation signal in the substrate, so nothing in this file is executable today and the objects it loads carry the gap as needs_signal patterns rather than pretending otherwise. Two claims here are the most likely to be argued with on review and should be: that unknown severity must fail toward attention rather than into a triage backlog, and that priority should be cheap to revise while severity is not. Both are defensible in a queue with slack and become expensive in one without it, which is the review question worth asking.
